31676-heathen-master-filcsik:
Kálmán Mikszáth's short story Heathen Master Filcsik comes into English from the Magyar in a translation by William N. Loew, printed at Cleveland at the Clerk's Private Press in 1910. An introductory note explains that Loew placed the manuscript at the publisher's disposal. It adds that the tale is one of the shorter stories of a living Hungarian writer.

The note adds that Magyar literature is a gold mine for translators, though few have explored it. Most first-class Hungarian authors besides the novelist Maurus Jókai remain unknown to the average American reader. Filcsik's tale is offered as a sample of that untranslated wealth.
britannica-1911-abel-niels-henrik:
Niels Henrik Abel receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abel, a Norwegian mathematician born at Findöe in 1802, proved his genius at Christiania's cathedral school by solving Holmboë's problems. A poor minister's son, he reached the university on a small state pension.

His proof that the quintic equation cannot be solved by radicals came first, in 1824. Travel in 1825 brought him to Crelle in Berlin and to Paris, where fame lagged and funds failed. Elliptic, hyperelliptic, and the new Abelian functions bear his mark. Crelle won him a Berlin post in 1829; the offer reached Norway after his death near Arendal. Legendre's praise heads the close: what a head that young Norwegian had.
britannica-1911-acharius-erik:
Erik Acharius (1757-1819) was a Swedish botanist who entered Upsala University in 1773 as a pupil of Linnaeus, the great classifier of plants. He took his medical degree at Lund in 1782 and became professor of botany at Wadstena Academy in 1801. The short Britannica biography gives a life narrowed to one devoted subject.

Lichens claimed all his work. Every publication Acharius produced dealt with that class of plants, the crusty growths formed by fungi and algae living together. His Lichenographia Universalis, published at Gottingen in 1804, is named as the most important of them. He died at Wadstena in 1819, having given lichen study its early system.
britannica-1911-ahmed-vefik:
Ahmed Vefik Pasha, Turkish statesman and man of letters of 1819 to 1891, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Stambul, he was the son of Rouheddin Effendi, a fine French scholar who served on Reshid Pasha's mission to Paris. Reshid took the boy along and schooled him there for about five years. Ahmed returned to a post in the foreign ministry's translation bureau.

In his spare hours he translated Moliere's plays into Turkish and compiled dictionaries and school manuals to spread French learning. He launched the Salnameh, the Ottoman official annual, in 1847, and served as imperial commissioner in the Danubian principalities. Briefly prime minister in 1878, he later governed Brusa for nearly four years. There he drained marshes, brought mountain water, built roads, suppressed brigandage, and multiplied schools.
britannica-1911-bilejik:
Bilejik, known in Byzantine times as Belocome, is a town in Asia Minor. It is the chief town of the Ertoghrul sanjak in the Brusa vilayet. The town stands on a hill at 1,900 feet above the sea. Its railway station, on the Ismid to Angora line, lies 22 miles away. The 1911 Britannica entry gives a population of 10,500. Of those people, 7,200 are listed as Moslems and 3,300 as Christians.

Silk is the town's key industry, the entry says. Several silk-spinning factories work there, making Bilejik an important centre of that trade. The entry runs to just three short sentences in total. It gives no history beyond the old Byzantine name. No buildings, markets, or leaders are named. The hill site, the mixed population, and the silk mills are the whole picture the text supports.
britannica-1911-birejik:
Birejik is a town of north-west Mesopotamia, in the Aleppo vilayet. It stands 1,170 feet up, on a limestone cliff 400 feet high. Below it runs the left bank of the Euphrates river. Its population is about 10,000, three-quarters of them Moslem. The town guards one of the Euphrates' most important crossings. A ferry now works the road from Aleppo toward Urfa, Diarbekr, and Mosul. In ancient times a bridge of boats crossed at the spot.

The place matches Apamea, which faced Zeugma across the river, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Its castle, Kala Beda, commanded the bridge and now lies much ruined. An older name, Birtha, came back under Roman rule and survives today. The emperor Julian rested there on his march in AD 363. The ferry ranked second only to Thapsacus for crossings south. A cruel massacre of Armenians there in 1895 closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beda-francisc:
Beda Franciscus Dudik was a Moravian historian born near Kremsier in 1815, who died as abbot and titular bishop at Raigern in 1890. After Brünn and Olmütz, he entered the Benedictines in 1836 and was ordained in 1840. He taught classics, then history, at Brünn's gymnasium until 1854. He became Vienna's Privatdozent in 1855, Moravia's historiographer in 1859, and an Academy member in 1865.

Research trips took him to Sweden, Rome, France, Belgium, Holland, and Russia, and he founded the Teutonic Order's historical library at Vienna. A prolific writer drawing on sources, he published histories of Raigern, Moravian sources, Waldstein, and the Teutonic Order's coins and treasures. His chief work, the twelve-volume general history of Moravia (1860-89), runs to 1350, with its Przemyslian volumes translated into Czech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eznik:
Eznik was a fifth-century Armenian writer, born at Golp in Taikh, a Chorokh tributary valley in north Armenia. He studied under Isaac the catholicos and Mesrop. At their request he traveled first to Edessa, then to Constantinople, to master the sciences and to gather Syriac and Greek manuscripts. He came home to Armenia after the Council of Ephesus in 431.

He is probably the Eznik, Bishop of Bagrevand, who sat in the Synod of Artashat in 449. Besides work on the new Bible version, he wrote his great treatise Against the Sects between 441 and 449. It holds four books: against heathens, against Parseeism, against Greek philosophers, and against Marcionism. He argues from the Bible more than from reason. He shows keen mind and wide learning, at home in Persian as in Greek letters, in choice classical Armenian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-von-pau:
Franz von Paula Hladnik, born at Idria in Carniola on 29 March 1773 and died at Laibach on 25 November 1844. He was an Austrian botanist and schoolmaster who built Laibach's schools and its flora. Son of a mining official, he studied philosophy and theology and was ordained priest in 1796. But weak health barred parish work, so that year he became scriptor in the Laibach Lyceum library, soon giving it up for forty years of teaching in Laibach schools. By 1803 he directed the Normal School, and from 1807 to failing sight he served as prefect of the gymnasium, which he brought to flourishing condition, earning the Emperor Francis's honourable distinction.

During the French occupation he became professor of botany and natural history in Laibach's Central School. He received land for a garden of Carniolan flora that soon held six hundred kinds of local plants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kaiserchronik:
The Kaiserchronik is a twelfth-century German epic poem, at once a legend of all the saints and a tangled history of emperors. It runs from Roman emperors through German kings and emperors to King Conrad III's crusade in 1147. Written about 1150, probably by an ecclesiastic of Ratisbon who backed the Guelphs, it is often ascribed to Konrad der Pfaffe, author of the Song of Roland. Its sources included the Chronicle of Ekkehard and the Annolied.

Twelve complete manuscripts and seventeen partial ones survive, proof of wide popularity, and the poem was continued twice in the thirteenth century. The original ended at verse 17,283; a Bavarian addition ran to 800 verses, and a Swabian one carried the story to the Interregnum of 1254 to 1273. Massmann published it in full between 1849 and 1854, but the best edition is Schröder's of 1892. Its language is fair and at times genuinely poetic.
